name: Human Papillomavirus Infections
system: Dermatologic / Mucocutaneous (with anogenital and aerodigestive involvement)

clinicalPearls: Warts are cutaneous neoplasms caused by human papillomaviruses (HPVs), of which more than 100 distinct types have been described (Harrison 22e p.1525).

Verruca vulgaris, the common wart, is typically a sessile, dome-shaped lesion roughly a centimeter across with a hyperkeratotic surface made up of many fine filamentous projections (Harrison 22e p.1525).

Plantar warts are endophytic and covered by thick keratin; paring them characteristically uncovers a central core of keratinized debris with punctate bleeding points, which helps distinguish them from corns (Harrison 22e p.1525).
Flat warts (verruca plana) are only slightly raised with a velvety, nonverrucous surface, favor the face, arms, and legs, and are frequently spread by shaving (Harrison 22e p.1525).
Filiform warts present as papillomatous lesions on a narrow base and are common on the face, neck, and skinfolds (Harrison 22e p.1525).

Genital warts start as small papillomas that can enlarge into large fungating lesions; in women they may involve the labia, perineum, perianal skin, and the vaginal, urethral, anal, and cervical mucosa, while in men they often begin in the coronal sulcus and may extend to the penile shaft, scrotum, perianal skin, or urethra (Harrison 22e p.1525).

HPV types 16 and 18 are the most intensively studied and are the major risk factors for intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, anus, vulva, and penis (Harrison 22e p.1525).
Sexual transmission of HPV is described as the fundamental etiologic factor for cervical cancer (Harrison 22e p.1602).

Persistent oral HPV infection, particularly HPV-16, raises the risk of oropharyngeal cancer even without smoking or alcohol use, and the increase appears greater than additive when HPV and smoking coexist; oral HPV is believed to be largely sexually acquired (Harrison 22e p.1601).
A highly effective HPV vaccine for selected types is FDA-approved and reduces the incidence of anogenital and cervical carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.1525).

The available nonavalent HPV vaccine covers strains 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58; types 6 and 11 cause genital papillomas while the remaining types drive cervical and anal cancer, and reduction of types 16 and 18 alone could theoretically prevent more than 70% of cervical cancers worldwide (Harrison 22e p.1601).
harrison.pathophysiology: Human papillomaviruses are DNA viruses that, like other papillomaviruses, gain entry through breaks in the skin and infect epithelial cells, producing benign cutaneous neoplasms (warts). Keratinized cells are not viable hosts for replication, so the virus targets viable epithelium at cutaneous and mucosal surfaces. More than 100 HPV types exist; certain oncogenic types (notably 16 and 18) integrate into host epithelium and drive intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, anus, vulva, and penis, and persistent oral HPV-16 promotes oropharyngeal carcinoma. Histology of affected sites may show changes of typical warts and/or features of intraepidermal carcinoma (Bowen's disease). The oncogenic potential is markedly amplified in immunosuppressed hosts (Harrison 22e p.1525, p.1601).
additionalDifferentials: Squamous cell carcinoma / intraepidermal carcinoma (Bowen's disease)
Condyloma lata of secondary syphilis (for anogenital lesions)
nonInfectiousMimics: Squamous cell carcinoma and intraepidermal carcinoma (Bowen's disease)
additionalInvestigations: Clinical recognition of lesion morphology (location, surface, punctate bleeding points after paring of plantar warts)
Skin/mucosal biopsy with histologic examination when malignancy is suspected (may show typical wart changes and/or intraepidermal carcinoma)
Cervical cytology (Pap smear) for cervical screening
HPV testing (with or without Pap smear), recommended beginning at age 30 per cited screening guidance
redFlags: Lesions in patients immunosuppressed after solid organ transplantation or with HIV, who carry higher risk of HPV-associated malignancy and warrant monitoring for squamous cell carcinoma and other cutaneous malignancies
Anogenital lesions showing histologic features of intraepidermal carcinoma (Bowen's disease)
Persistent or growing fungating anogenital masses
New oropharyngeal lesions in the setting of persistent HPV-16, particularly with concurrent tobacco use
harrison.prognosis: Most warts in normal (immunocompetent) individuals resolve spontaneously within 1-2 years. However, oncogenic HPV types, especially 16 and 18, can lead to intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, anus, vulva, penis, and oropharynx, with higher risk in immunosuppressed patients. The HPV vaccine is highly effective at preventing persistent strain-specific infection and preneoplastic lesions (cervical or anal intraepithelial neoplasia grades I-III) in individuals not previously infected, though it does not affect established infections (Harrison 22e p.1525, p.1601).
pitfalls: Assuming all warts require aggressive treatment: most resolve spontaneously within 1-2 years in healthy people (Harrison 22e p.1525).
Overlooking the malignant potential of oncogenic HPV types and failing to monitor immunosuppressed (transplant or HIV) patients for squamous cell carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.1525).
Expecting the HPV vaccine to clear existing infection: it does not appear to affect preexisting infections (Harrison 22e p.1601).
Screening cervical cytology more frequently than recommended adds little benefit and can cause harm through unnecessary procedures and overtreatment of transient lesions (Harrison 22e p.1602).
harrison.severityClassification: HPV-associated cervical and anal disease is described histologically as intraepithelial neoplasia graded I, II, and III (CIN/AIN), reflecting progressive preneoplastic change preceding invasive squamous cell carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.1601).
management: Treat cutaneous and genital warts with ablative or destructive methods such as cryotherapy, topical salicylic acid, podophyllotoxin or trichloroacetic acid
Use topical immunomodulators such as imiquimod for genital warts, with surgical or laser removal and electrocautery for large or refractory lesions
Prevent infection and HPV-related cancers with prophylactic HPV vaccination
Undertake cervical screening with cytology and HPV testing, with colposcopy and treatment such as large-loop excision of intraepithelial neoplasia
Screen and monitor anal, vulval, penile and oropharyngeal sites, and refer confirmed carcinoma to oncology
Recognise heightened oncogenic risk in immunosuppressed patients and intensify surveillance accordingly
Counsel that most warts in immunocompetent people regress spontaneously, offering reassurance and expectant management where appropriate
